units.title: Something my son said about the stairs
units.author: dc_11_soraya
units.text: Not a complaint, just sharing because I'm tired and it's been on my mind. R. is six. With the lift out we walk down from 11 every morning. Today on the landing at 7 he stopped and said 'the man on the stairs waits for us'. I asked which man. He said the one who waits. Little M. laughed. I assume it's a story from school. Has anyone else's child said anything like it?

units.author: dc_12_ollie
units.text: my mum says its probably from the year 9s at school, theres a story going round that Dellow has a man on the stairs who counts you. i dont know who started it. it wasnt me. does R go to St Bede's? the little kids there hear everything from the big kids on the bus

units.author: dellow_admin
units.text: Thanks Soraya, and thanks Ollie. Gentle reminder to everyone that little ones read this board over our shoulders sometimes, so please keep it kind and keep it factual. Ollie, I'll check with your mum that you're still allowed on here. The lift part is apparently on order. Bev, DCRA

units.author: dc_6_jordie
units.text: lol the man on the stairs is me at 2am coming back from the lab, I wait on landings because the cardio of doom has killed my legs. but sincerely, R. sounds like a smart kid, and kids pick up on the adults being jumpy. if he wants I'll do the stairs with you one morning and do the silly walk. it works on my little cousin.

units.author: dc_8_benedikt
units.text: I do not want to make it worse. But I will say I also stop on 7 sometimes when the light goes, and I listen. I have not seen any man. I tell my nephew if he is scared on stairs to sing loud. Then you hear only yourself. Maybe it is useful for R. too. Sorry for my spelling.

units.author: dc_14_ivy
units.text: For what it's worth (not much, I'm an illustrator), when I was R.'s age I was certain a woman lived in our boiler cupboard and judged my handwriting. She didn't. (She did, a bit.) Kids build a person out of whatever the dark gives them. Up here on 14 the stairwell does make some very personable noises at night.

units.title: Lift: part on order, and torches
units.author: dellow_admin
units.text: Update from Kerrow Estates by phone today: the lift engineer says it's the door controller and the part is 'on order'. No date. I asked for one and was thanked for my patience. I am out of patience, but I'm passing it on. Anyone who needs shopping carried, post here and someone will help. Bev, DCRA

units.author: dc_2_hassan
units.text: I still have torches in the shop at cost price, the small ones with a clip, and batteries. For anyone over 70 or with small children, one free while stocks last, just ask at the till. I can also leave bread outside doors on the upper floors in the morning if you message me before 22:00. H

units.author: dc_7_irena
units.text: Dear Hassan, thank you, I will gladly take one of the clip torches and pay for it, as I am perfectly able to. My late husband always kept one in his coat pocket and I have never replaced his. It is time. Irena, 7C

units.title: Sketch: the 7th floor landing, 2 a.m.
units.author: dc_14_ivy
units.text: Did a quick sketch of the landing on 7 while my kettle boiled (well, after, I'm not that fast). Charcoal: the fire door half shut, the push button glowing green like a little planet, the window black, and the bottom step of the next flight going up into nothing because that's where the light stops. No figures. It didn't need one.

units.author: dc_6_jordie
units.text: ivy this is genuinely beautiful and genuinely the last thing I wanted to see at 2am before going down to the laundry room. 10/10 would be scared again. the green button really is the only friend you have in there

units.author: dc_14_ivy
units.text: Sorry (not sorry). In the interest of balance I'll draw the laundry room next, which is objectively the least frightening room in the building, unless you've seen what machine 2 does to wool. Also: if you're going down now, can you check if the light on 12 is stuck on again? It's shining under my door.

units.title: Brackwater, night in fog: footpath only (raw files)
units.author: dunlin_rec
units.text: As promised to the estate, last night I stayed on the public footpath on the east ride. Fog came down around 01:00. Two omnis on a stand, gain -12, low cut 80 Hz; handheld as backup. The fog flattens everything: the dam outflow, normally loud, is a soft hiss. At 02:41 there are three knocks, further off than last time and dull, as if wrapped. Files attached. Make of it what you will.

units.author: tern_audio
units.text: ok so 02:41 again-ish?? that's weirdly close to your first night. the attack on these is softer, but that could just be the fog eating the top end, there's a lot less above 2k. spectrogram tomorrow. also I'm going to the pumping house end this week with my recorder, if the fog lets me find the road

units.author: skeptic_hollis
units.text: Quick look. The fog doesn't eat high frequencies as much as people think; humidity actually helps them a bit. What changes is the temperature layering, which bends sound and changes what reaches you. The softer attack points to a longer path. My water hammer suggestion still stands: valve cycling at the outflow around the same time each night would explain your regularity.

units.author: dunlin_rec
units.text: Fair, Hollis, and the regular timing is the strongest point for something mechanical. I've written to the water company asking whether the outflow valves run on a timer. The direction doesn't help you, though: the dish puts these north, into the trees, and the outflow is south-west. But a fog bending sound could muddle that. I'll wait for the reply.

units.author: hobby_hydrophone
units.text: Three dull knocks at a fixed hour near a reservoir. That's a pump. Or a valve. Or a pump driving a valve. Somebody somewhere has a timer set to 02:40 and a bad bearing. It's always a pump.

units.author: lowband_mod
units.text: Good post, and thank you for staying on the footpath. Reminder to everyone joining in: comment on the files, not on what you imagine is out there. If you want to argue pump versus deer versus anything else, say what in the recording supports it. dunlin, tag these with the fog conditions so the catalogue picks them up.

units.title: How sound carries over water in fog (short version)
units.author: hobby_hydrophone
units.text: Everyone's about to record fog this week, so: over cold water with warmer air on top, sound refracts down and travels far, and it arrives from slightly wrong directions. Boat engines a mile off sound close. Moorings knock. Hulls slap. A ferry horn wanders left and right. Before you post 'mysterious knock, harbour, night', check the tide and what's moored nearby.

units.author: hobby_tapeloop
units.text: A very useful note, thank you. I would add that tape recorded in fog often shows more hiss than it should, because people turn the gain up to catch distant sounds and the machine hears itself instead. I made that mistake for twenty years. I still have the tapes to prove it. Regards, Ned

units.author: tern_audio
units.text: ok so this is really helpful, saving it. does the same thing happen over a reservoir or does it need to be the sea? Brackwater reservoir was steaming tonight and I could hear the substation hum from the school car park, which is like two km

units.author: hobby_hydrophone
units.text: Same physics, smaller scale. Cold water, still air, layer on top. A reservoir in a valley is even better for it because the hills keep the wind off. Two km for a substation hum is easy on a night like this. So is the dam outflow. So is a pump.

units.title: Log: figure on monitor 6, nil found on patrol
units.author: lh_dockguard_coriveth
units.text: Gate 7, container port. 01:12 monitor 6 (NE yard camera) shows a figure standing at the edge of the lot, just where the floodlight ends. Static. Radioed control, walked over, on site 01:16. Patrolled, nil found. No vehicle, no one on the fence line. Back in the hut at 01:24, monitor 6 shows the lot empty. Logged. Posting because it's 3am and I wanted to tell someone.

units.author: skeptic_dmitra
units.text: Glad you told someone. Two boring possibilities. One: a lens artefact. Floodlit cameras pointing into a dark area often show a smeared bright blob at the boundary, especially with condensation on the housing, which a body-shaped brain then reads as a person. Two: a real person who left before you arrived. Four minutes is a long time. Does the camera record, or just display?

units.author: lh_dockguard_coriveth
units.text: Records, 7 days loop. Reviewed it. Figure visible 01:11:40 to 01:15:05, then gone between two frames. No walking off. Camera housing was dry, I checked, it's under the canopy. I take the point about four minutes. A person could leave in four minutes. They'd leave in the frames though.

units.author: lh_security_st
units.text: Cameras drop frames all the time when the recorder's busy, ours does it whenever more than eight channels have motion. Check if the timestamps are evenly spaced around 01:15. If there's a jump of a second or two, someone could walk out of shot in the gap. Not saying that's it. Saying it's the first thing Control would ask me.

units.author: hollow_signal
units.text: The edge of the light... that's always where they stand, isn't it. You'll see more of this. Not just at your port. I've said too much already.

units.author: lh_mod
units.text: Housekeeping: HollowSignal, this is the first and friendly warning. Lamp Hours is company on the night shift, not campfire stories, and 'I've said too much' posts aren't company. Gate7, thanks for a clear log. If it happens again, Dev's frame question is the right one to check. Drink some water, everyone.

units.author: lh_dockguard_coriveth
units.text: Checked. Timestamps run 01:15:04, 01:15:05, 01:15:07. There is a skipped second. So, possible. Noted in the book for IT, who are day shift only. Patrolled NE yard again 03:30, nil found. Thank you both.

units.title: The van, again. Control has a theory.
units.author: lh_security_st
units.text: It came back tonight. White panel van, same spot at the far edge of the car park lights, engine running from about 23:40, headlights off. Control says it's a sleeping driver, we've had them before, leave him be. Fine. At 00:20 I walked up with the torch and knocked on the window. The cab was empty. Engine running, nobody in the seats.

units.author: lh_picker_weyhaven
units.text: Bloke's in the back on a sleeping bag, Dev. Half the agency drivers at our depot kip in the load bay with the engine on for the heater, it's cheaper than a room. Then they're out at five to make their first drop. Doesn't explain why your one picks your car park, but it explains the empty cab.

units.author: lh_security_st
units.text: That's genuinely the most likely answer and I feel a bit silly. The bulkhead's solid so I couldn't see into the back. I didn't knock on the side, because if there's a man asleep in there, I'm not waking him to ask if he's real. Logged as 'vehicle, idling, occupant not seen'. Control is delighted with me.

units.author: lh_porter_portammet
units.text: Night porter's rule: never knock on the side of anything that's humming. Not vans, not freezers, not the morgue fridge. Respect the hum. Good log though, Dev. 'Occupant not seen' is going on the B corridor whiteboard as our new motto.

units.title: Intercom update (it's still doing it)
units.author: lh_nurse_halvard
units.text: Update for the people who asked. The bay intercom called his name again at 03:05 tonight, same voice, same bed number. Maintenance came this afternoon, pressed every button and said 'can't reproduce'. The charge nurse has now put a strip of tape over the panel as if that helps. The sticky note is still there. He's fine, he's at his daughter's. Back to it.

units.author: skeptic_dmitra
units.text: Still betting on a stuck or intermittent call button. They fail with damp and temperature, so they'll trigger at the coldest part of the night and test fine at 2pm. The system stores the bed's last registered patient until someone updates it, hence the old name. Ask maintenance whether the bed record was ever cleared after discharge. I'd bet a coffee it wasn't.

units.author: lh_nurse_halvard
units.text: You may well be right, Dmitra. I asked our ward clerk and she went pale and said 'oh'. So that's a probable. The bed record update has gone in. It doesn't explain why it only goes at three, but I'm told the heating drops at three. I'll owe you a coffee if it stops. Back to it.

units.title: helpline nights, week two (anonymised, with love)
units.author: lh_callcentre_tamsin
units.text: night four of this run. caller one: a man who wanted to know if he could pay his bill 'in instalments of one'. sir. that's just paying it. caller two: a lady whose fridge is 'making a noise like it's thinking'. I asked what it was thinking about. she said 'leaving'. I said that's the compressor, madam, it's fine. she said that's what my husband said.

units.author: lh_callcentre_tamsin
units.text: caller three, between my coffee and my other coffee: a teenager asking if the power company can 'turn the streetlight back on' outside his house because his mum says he can't walk the dog in the dark. it's a council light, kid. I gave him the number. he said thanks. he said the dog is called Pudding. I needed that.

units.author: lh_trucker_orrin
units.text: Hana, you got the best job on the forum and the worst hold music, I've heard it. Pudding's a good name for a dog. My old rig dog was called Diesel and he'd ride shotgun with his head out from here to the state line. Coffee number two's the important one, by the way. Drink it slow.

units.title: fares of the week (halvard edition)
units.author: lh_taxi_halvard
units.text:
fare one picked up at the hospital rank, a man carrying a goldfish in a bag, said he couldn't leave it at home alone on its birthday
fare two two students arguing about whether a hot dog is a sandwich all the way to the river, I said no and got a bad tip
fare three my favourite, a nurse off shift who fell asleep before I'd turned the meter on, so I didn't. anyway

units.author: lh_nurse_halvard
units.text: I know exactly who fare three was and she says thank you, and that she will tip properly next time when she is conscious. The goldfish man is a legend on the respiratory ward; he brings the fish to visit his father. Back to it.

units.author: lh_taxi_halvard
units.text: small world, the city's a village after midnight. the fish is called Captain apparently, he told me on the way out, and I said happy birthday Captain and he said Captain doesn't like a fuss. anyway, quiet one now, the rank's empty and the cafe on the corner has its chairs up, so it's me and the radio

units.title: Customers, ranked
units.author: lh_convenience_kestrel
units.text: 1. The man who buys one egg every night. One. 2. The cyclist who asks for the toilet code and then doesn't go. 3. Two schoolgirls doing homework at the coffee counter at 1am, who should be in bed, who I gave free buns. 4. Me, who buys my own dinner from the hot cabinet at 4 and judges myself.

units.author: lh_student_kestrel
units.text: I am the girl who buys three energy drinks and a single banana at 2am 'for balance'. please put me on the list. also I will be in tonight. the lab is freezing and the corridor lights keep doing their thing where they turn on for nobody, which honestly is the most attention I've had all week

units.author: lh_convenience_kestrel
units.text: You're number 5. The banana is a lie we both agree to. Corridor lights turning on for nobody: our forecourt sensor does it for moths. Big moths. Ask your facilities people about moths.

units.title: End of shift, from the bus
units.author: lh_miner_vellmark
units.text: Shift done. Pump on level 4 tripped twice, both times on the hour, fixed with a hammer and a word I won't write. Up top it's minus three and the town hasn't woken. The baker's light is on. Bus driver's the same one as yesterday, he's started nodding at me. That's a relationship, up here.

units.author: lh_carer_vellmark
units.text: I'm on the next bus up from the home in twenty minutes, so put the kettle on. Quiet night here. Mrs A. slept right through for once, and Mr D. told me about his wedding again, which I didn't mind, because the cake gets bigger every time. I'm sorry, this is a long post for 'put the kettle on'.

units.title: What are you reading at 3 a.m.?
units.author: lh_insomniac_tollinby
units.text: Gentle question for the small hours. I have the shop's worst-selling novel open, a sea story in which nobody reaches land for four hundred pages, and I find I don't want them to. Outside it's fog, and the Carrow Point signal is just audible from Tollinby, which I didn't know was possible. What's on your bedside table, or your dashboard, or your break-room counter?

units.author: lh_porter_portammet
units.text: The A&E noticeboard, mostly. Tonight's highlight: 'Whoever keeps taking the blue pens, we know.' A thriller in nine words. Also a crossword in the porters' room that nobody's finished since 2019. Can hear your foghorn from the hospital roof when I go up for a breather, by the way. Sounds like a cow that's lost its friend.

units.author: lh_lighttender_tamsin
units.text: A tide almanac, which I read the way some people read poetry, and an old keeper's memoir lent by a colleague, which I read slowly because the keeper writes slowly. He says the hours just before dawn are the longest on a light, because the beam has been going round so long that you stop seeing it and start seeing only what it doesn't reach.

units.title: Carrow Point fog signal: how far can you hear it?
units.author: lh_insomniac_tollinby
units.text: Small survey, if anyone's awake. I'm in Tollinby, which is a good twenty kilometres inland, and I can hear the Carrow Point signal tonight from my bedroom window, very faint, every thirty seconds. I didn't think that was possible. Where are you, and can you hear it?

units.author: wx_carrowpoint
units.text: Up past my bedtime, but this is my subject. Under a strong inversion like tonight's, low-frequency sound can travel absurd distances, and the signal is designed to carry. Twenty kilometres is entirely possible on a still night with fog. From here it rattles the cups. Thank you for the data point: Tollinby, faint, every thirty seconds.

units.author: gilliver_lamp
units.text: Gilliver, and yes, very clear, as it always has been. When I was a girl we counted it to get to sleep, and my brother used to say the island answered it. It doesn't. It is only the echo coming off the Holm cliffs. But it does sound like an answer if you are seven.
